content: *I wander around the square, looking at the market stalls*

speaker: narrator
content: The strip of awnings between the war memorial and the market hall smells of wet canvas and winter greens; a stallholder in a flat cap is weighing potatoes on a brass scale while a woman ahead of him counts change twice, unhurried. The clock on the old hall shows half past ten and always will, four minutes behind everyone else's, and the cobbles underfoot are dry but cold, with grit and cabbage leaves tracked across them from the Tuesday rain. Somewhere behind the cheese stall a dog is barking at nothing in particular.

speaker: player
content: *I wander in the direction of the tearoom*

speaker: narrator
content: (Sam leaves for Marsh's Tea Room.)

speaker: narrator
content: (The scene moves to Marsh's Tea Room.)

speaker: narrator
content: The door swings shut behind Sam and the steam off the kettle fogs the glass further, so the square outside goes soft and grey. Eight tables, several of them taken, and a glass cabinet of scones and parkin by the counter, where Maureen Marsh is lifting a tray of something out of the oven, flour to her elbow in her cardigan sleeve. By the door the noticeboard is thick with lost cats, piano lessons and a parish newsletter, and the room smells of tea, sugar and hot fat.

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Now then, love — come in, come in, shut that door behind you or we'll have all t'square in. You'll be the one at number 9, then. I heard there was a moving van up Tanner's Row Tuesday. *wipes hands on the apron.* Sit yourself down, it's parkin day and the kettle's not long boiled. Tea?

speaker: player
content: Yes...please. What gave me away?

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Oh, love, you've flour on your sleeve and removal-van dust on your shoulders, and you've that look on you like a lamb that's wandered into t'wrong field. Besides, I've been watching that street all week — a van on Tuesday, curtains twitching since. Sit down, do.

speaker: player
content: Very well. I see nothing gets past you. *I sit.* Do you run this place alone?

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Alone? Give over — I've Kez, she's in five days a week, been with me two years come January. She's not here this minute, mind. But mostly it's me and the kettle, and the kettle's the better company. Been at this thirty-one years, so I'd say we rub along. Why, were you after a job?

speaker: player
content: No, no. Just curious. Tea and something to eat would be lovely

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Right then — a pot of tea for two, since I'm having one whether you like it or not, and you'll have a scone with it and a bit of parkin on the side, warm from oven. No arguing. Now then, what brings you up to Marlbeck from that London? Work, was it?

speaker: player
content: No, no. Just needed to get out of the city

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Aye, well. Cities'll do that to you. *sets the pot down.* There's worse places to land than Marlbeck, I'll say that much. It's quiet, mind — nobody'll hurry you and nobody'll leave you be, neither, so you'll have to pick which one you can live with. Milk and sugar?

speaker: player
content: Please, both

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: There we are — milk and one sugar, and if it's too strong for you, say so, I don't stand on ceremony. *pours.* Now then. You've got the house, you've got the tea. What else have you got? A job to go to, or are you going to be at a loose end come Monday?

speaker: player
content: I've got something, but it isn't starting for a week or so. *I take a sip.* Pretty good

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Good, that's the way I like it — a bit of body to it, none of your dishwater. *sits down opposite.* So what is it, then, this something that doesn't start till next week? Don't leave me hanging, love, I've a whole café to tell it to after you've gone.

speaker: player
content: It's positively indecent, I warn you. Taxes

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Taxes! *laughs.* Well, that's the first time anyone's called taxes indecent in my café and meant it as a joke. Go on then — are you an inspector, or is it summat duller like doing other people's for them? Because if it's the first, I'll be wanting me receipts in order, and if it's the second, half of Marlbeck'll be at your door by Sunday.

speaker: player
content: I'm just an accountant, Nothing too romantic

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: An accountant. *grins.* Well, I'm disappointed now, I'd had you down as summat exciting. Still, every town needs one and ours has been making do with a man in Skipton who takes three weeks to answer a letter, so you'll be a novelty. Where are you set up, then — here in town, or are you off to Skipton on the bus every morning?

speaker: player
content: No, I can work out of the house for the time being

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Working from home. Now I'm jealous — I've not had a quiet hour to meself since 1995. Mind, that house of yours, you'll get more quiet than you bargained for. Tanner's Row's a street where you can hear a kettle boil three doors down.

speaker: player
content: I'm hardly here looking for hustle and bustle. It'll work out

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Aye, that's the right way to look at it. Marlbeck'll not rush you and it'll not judge you, and if you want to be left alone of an evening, you will be. *sips her tea.* Mind, don't go being too much of a stranger. Half of what's good about this town happens in other people's kitchens.

speaker: player
content: I think I'll leave people to what they get up to in their own kitchen

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Ha! Well, that's you told, Maureen. *sits back.* Suit yourself, love — but I'll warn you now, in this town it's the other way round. You'll be sat in your kitchen minding your own business and somebody'll knock on with a bit of sponge and a question about your pipes. There's no stopping it. Best just to open the door and get it over with.

speaker: player
content: My pipes? Do people often enquire about one another's pipes?

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Pipes, aye — has nobody warned you? Come January this town freezes solid and every pipe in Tanner's Row starts complaining. So folk knock on, ostensibly about your pipes, and then they stay for an hour and tell you what's wrong with the council. It's the plumbing that gets them through the door, love. The tea does the rest.

speaker: player
content: What is wrong with the council?

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Oh, where do I start. Bins, for one — they moved us to fortnightly collection and half the town's been writing letters since. Arthur Bell at number eleven, your neighbour, he'll tell you all about it given half a chance, he writes to them about twice a month and they write back about twice a year. And the clock in the square's four minutes slow, has been since before the war, and the council won't touch it. Some say it's a listed eccentricity. I say they've just never noticed it's wrong.

speaker: player
content: They won't adjust the clock? But surely they change it twice a year for daylight saings?

speaker: maureen-marsh
content: Oh, that's the joke of it — they do, twice a year, somebody goes up that ladder and turns it. And it's still four minutes slow afterward! Every single time. It's like it's decided, the clock has, and it's not shifting for any of us. My Les used to set his watch by it and then add the four, and he'd still be late.

speaker: player
content: How odd
